headings.title: From launcher intent to application runtime
Profile identity, pending generations and publication

html:
Compiled launch and dependency generations

A compiled Server or Gateway keeps first-party modules in its application image and third-party Python packages in a shared, versioned environment. The bootstrap selects that environment before entering the normal application. Repair prepares a separate generation so a failed attempt before publication can leave the previous environment available.

This page covers the compiled entry point, dependency installer and native prerequisites. Build and installation instructions remain the operator reference. Setup primitives explain paths, acceptance, locks, verified downloads and permission repair. The inference-portal role delegates to its own bootstrap; application updates, registration, service management and removal have separate lifecycle owners. The installation-state guide follows resource records, process identities and bounded removal after setup.

From launcher intent to application runtime

configure requires the compiled-shared-v1 backend marker in build-info.json, records explicit process context and prepends the image's modules directory. It disables bytecode writes and supplies a default shared browser location. This is configuration after launcher handoff, not an independent authenticity check.

The entry point consumes bootstrap flags and preserves unknown arguments for the application. It derives Server variant or Gateway instance defaults, validates lifecycle options and delegates those workflows. Legal display and help do not install dependencies. Dependency status reads receipts and file sizes; it does not re-run feature checks. Server owner-account setup/reset has a separate early branch.

flowchart TD Entry[Explicit compiled application root] --> Role{Inference portal?} Role -->|Yes| Portal[Delegate to portal bootstrap] Role -->|No| Parse[Parse bootstrap flags and select role / instance] Parse --> Early{Early action?} Early -->|Legal display / auth / help / maintenance / status| Owner[Delegate to its owner and return] Early -->|Application child| Child[Apply recorded runtime context and enter application] Early -->|Ordinary launch| Need[Read registration and dependency readiness] Need --> ServiceNeed{Service needs setup?} ServiceNeed -->|Yes| Refuse[Stop and request interactive repair] ServiceNeed -->|No| Preflight{Native preflight?} Preflight -->|Yes| Code[Return 76 if setup needed, otherwise 0] Preflight -->|No| Service{Service invocation?} Service -->|Ready service| Stored[Validate recorded interpreter and managed core marker] Service -->|Ordinary user| Setup[Confirm if needed and select or prepare dependencies] Stored --> Launch[Launch application in selected runtime] Setup --> Register[Register installation under lifecycle lock] Register --> Only{Setup or dependency repair only?} Only -->|Yes| Done[Return without starting application] Only -->|No| Launch

The diagram groups routing branches; it is not a substitute for the parser's exact precedence. The service-needs-setup guard runs before native preflight. Lifecycle registration and environment selection run under the installation-store lock. Managed dependency creation has its own inner dependencies.lock. The maintenance guard is checked for setup/repair/needed work. Services use the recorded environment and refuse automatic installation; their managed-runtime check requires the interpreter and a core marker, without repeating the complete profile readiness check.

Ordinary startup calls ensure_environment, which rejects running the application as root/administrator before considering reuse. An unapproved, non-repair managed launch can return immediately from the read-only readiness check. Otherwise it obtains invocation acceptance and enters the scoped directory-repair context. Explicit acceptance is either two terminal answers or both matching --accept-license VERSION and --accept-eula VERSION flags. --yes and --non-interactive alone do not accept terms. Acceptance is local to the invocation; the legal owner records the exact bundled document versions and hashes.

After setup, POSIX uses execv to replace the bootstrap process. Windows waits for a child so the native supervisor retains its process/job ownership. The internal --run-application branch restores recorded runtime environment and arguments, opens the running-instance context and invokes the role's update-recovery hook before application entry. Without a registration record it enters the application directly. Application exceptions retain application handling rather than being converted into setup errors.

worker_command builds isolated UTF-8 Python argv with -I -B, the bundled worker bootstrap and each original argument as a separate value. worker routes specific installation/job/terminal helpers to their entry points, known package prefixes to main, and other modules through runpy. It is a dispatch helper, not a module allowlist or permission boundary. No shell string is assembled.

Profile identity, pending generations and publication

profile requires a nonempty schema-v1 Python lock and hashes it together with bundled system-packages.json and native-downloads.json when present. Changing a native recipe therefore changes the profile namespace even if Python dependencies are identical. The hash identifies selected bundled input; it does not authenticate its producer.

Record or path Responsibility
installation/<profile>.json Published environment and its last completed dependency result.
installation/<profile>.pending.json Pointer to a resumable generation being prepared.
installation/<generation>.json Current attempt's stages, events and failures.
environments/<profile>/<generation>/.venv-created Venv creation completed; an interpreter alone is insufficient.
.core-ready inside the generation Mandatory checks completed for the matching profile identity.
smto-installation.json inside the generation Completed setup state copied into that environment.
installed-bom.json inside the generation Observed Python distributions, native package receipts and selected client evidence.
smto-paths.json and smto-browser.json Native search directories and an observed managed browser location.
sequenceDiagram participant Caller as Accepted setup invocation participant Installer as Dependency installer participant Lock as Dependency lock participant Records as Profile / pending / generation records participant Env as Selected generation Caller->>Installer: Ensure environment, optionally repair Installer->>Lock: Acquire dependencies.lock Installer->>Records: Read published and pending status alt Reusable ready / partial generation and no repair Installer->>Env: Check namespace, interpreter and matching core marker Installer->>Installer: Select existing environment else Prepare or repair Installer->>Records: Drop pending pointer if it names the published live generation Installer->>Records: Reuse valid pending path or publish a new generation pointer Installer->>Env: Resume venv and run dependency stages alt Mandatory stages and evidence collection succeed Installer->>Env: Write BOM, core marker and environment receipt Installer->>Records: Write generation log, then replace profile receipt Installer->>Records: Remove pending pointer Installer->>Env: Remove temporary build environment and source copies Installer->>Installer: Select ready or partial environment else Failure inside staged setup Installer->>Records: Record failed generation log Installer->>Installer: Retain failure to propagate end end Note over Installer,Records: Atomic JSON replacement is not a multi-file transaction Installer->>Lock: Release on scope exit Installer-->>Caller: Selected environment or propagated failure

A ready or partial environment is reusable only when its receipt points inside the current profile namespace, its interpreter exists and .core-ready contains that profile's identity. This lightweight check does not rehash every installed package or rerun optional verification. Malformed JSON and filesystem errors propagate. A plain warm return can be quiet; the locked reuse path reports retained optional failures when reached in an approved invocation.

A pending generation is reused in place. Its recorded path must remain within the profile's generation directory, then private-directory checks apply. Stages restart from the beginning, using completed markers and cached inputs where supported; this is not instruction-level continuation. The in-memory event list starts fresh for each attempt rather than merging earlier logs. The build-requirements marker is written only after its pinned installation succeeds.

Before the profile receipt is replaced, a failed repair leaves the prior published environment selected. Publication itself spans several writes: a failure after the profile replacement can leave the new profile selected while the generation log reports failure or cleanup is unfinished. There is no multi-file rollback or fsync durability guarantee. When a later repair finds a pending pointer naming the already-published environment, it removes that stale pointer before choosing new work, avoiding repair in the live generation. Earlier generations are retained; this installer does not garbage-collect them.

With no published receipt, environment_status exposes a pending generation log if available, otherwise not-installed. With a published receipt it keeps that status and attaches pending_setup. Disk sizes sum observed non-symlink file sizes under shared categories; they are neither allocated disk blocks nor an atomic snapshot.

Installation stages and failure policy

flowchart TD Venv[Create or resume venv] --> Core[Install pinned core wheels] Core --> Native[Attempt platform prerequisites and record failures] Native --> Paths[Record native directories and configure process environment] Paths --> Wheels[Try additional wheels as a group] Wheels --> Retry{Group failed?} Retry -->|Yes| Each[Retry each optional wheel separately] Retry -->|No| Source[Build allowlisted source packages] Each --> Source Source --> Tools[Attempt file finder, Chromium and eligible browser libraries] Tools --> Optional[Attempt browser / rendering / dependency / feature checks] Optional --> Required[Require core imports, inference check when enabled, readiness and file finder] Required --> Evidence[Collect distribution and client evidence] Evidence --> State{Any recorded optional failures?} State -->|Yes| Partial[Publish partial: core usable, repair needed] State -->|No| Ready[Publish ready]

Mandatory stage or evidence-collection failures propagate to the outer failed-log handler. Optional callbacks catch Exception and SystemExit, record a failed-step label and continue; KeyboardInterrupt still aborts. Stage-log publication occurs before that callback handler, so a log write failure is not converted into an optional dependency failure. Native installation returns handled failures as data; unexpected errors can still abort setup.

install_wheels writes direct URL/hash requirements and runs pip with no index, no dependency resolution, required hashes, binary-only inputs and no bytecode. Direct URLs can still need network access. The subprocess environment removes ambient Python/pip/Conda and compiler settings while retaining proxy/TLS choices; this is configuration isolation, not a security sandbox. pip_command also forwards SSL_CERT_FILE and selects the shared pip cache.

Only pygobject, pycairo and gssapi are allowed source builds. They use a separate venv with pinned build dependencies, verified source archives and native compilers. Previously built local dependencies are installed into that build venv; PyGObject is ordered after the other source packages. A successful build must produce exactly one wheel, whose actual digest and original source digest are recorded. Temporary build tools and source copies are removed after successful publication.

File-finder installation is attempted as an optional step so other diagnostics can run, but the final core/readiness/file-finder checks are mandatory. When enabled by build metadata, packaged inference imports are also mandatory. partial means mandatory checks passed and one or more optional steps/checks failed; it does not mean that every advertised feature is ready. --skip-system-deps contributes an explicit failed-step description and can still lead to a mandatory check failure if required tools are absent.

Browser setup uses the shared browser root. Chromium download, eligible Linux APT system libraries, browser verification and visualization setup have separate steps. The browser receipt is written only after the reported file exists. Process setup preserves an existing BROWSER_PATH, so that override can still affect consumers. A later visualization failure may leave the valid browser receipt in place.

Platform-native prerequisites

flowchart TD Recipes[Bundled system and native recipes] --> Skip{Skip requested?} Skip -->|Yes| Partial[Return skipped-step failure and no native receipts] Skip -->|No| Platform{Platform} Platform -->|Windows| Win[Private Docker clients and missing command recipes] Win --> Winget{winget available?} Winget -->|Yes| Packages[Install selected package IDs and collect evidence] Winget -->|No| Pinned[Run pinned upstream installer] Platform -->|macOS| Manager[Prefer existing Homebrew, otherwise MacPorts] Manager --> Found{Manager found?} Found -->|No| Brew[Attempt pinned Homebrew bootstrap] Found -->|Yes| Mac[Install configured recipes] Brew --> Recheck{Manager now found?} Recheck -->|Yes| Mac Recheck -->|No| Result Mac --> PG[MacPorts: build missing PostgreSQL clients when needed] Platform -->|Other POSIX branch| Linux[Select apt-get / dnf / yum / zypper / pacman] Linux --> Supported{Manager found?} Supported -->|No| Result Supported -->|Yes| Auth{Required authorization available?} Auth -->|No| Result Auth -->|Yes| Native[Attempt individual packages] Native --> Docker[On Linux: supply missing private Docker clients] Packages --> Result[Return receipts and handled failures] Pinned --> Result PG --> Result Docker --> Result

The platform diagram shows the successful branch shape. No supported Linux manager, failed authorization or unsuccessful macOS manager discovery returns explicit failures early. The macOS bootstrap proceeds to recipes only if a manager is found on the subsequent search. Package command failures are collected per step; malformed recipes and some unhandled errors propagate.

  • Windows: pinned private Docker, Compose and Buildx files are stored under the data root. The Docker archive contributes only the named client member. Existing per-user plugin files are preserved, and receipts distinguish the private file from its discovery path. Missing configured commands use winget or a pinned upstream installer. The PostgreSQL recipe selects command-line tools. Interactive upstream installation uses UAC and waits up to thirty minutes; timeout does not terminate an installer that is still running.
  • macOS: search includes Finder-missing Homebrew/MacPorts paths and prefers Homebrew if both are available. No manager triggers a pinned Homebrew bootstrap attempt. MacPorts uses the selected sudo policy and noninteractive package questions. If PostgreSQL clients remain missing, the private source fallback builds only libpq and client targets, checks the expected executable set and records source/license/file evidence.
  • Linux: choose the first supported available manager in the order shown. Yum uses DNF recipes. APT updates its package index and probes the available 7-Zip package name; the other branches use their configured install flags. Private x86_64 Docker clients fill missing commands without an engine fallback. Existing working clients are reused, with Compose required to report v2 or newer. TAR extraction selects exactly one regular docker/docker member.

The package recipes are the current package-name authority. This module does not add service-start commands or perform an explicit distribution upgrade; package managers still have their normal system side effects and package scripts. Those effects are not rolled back if Python setup fails later. Receipts collect available version/path evidence, not a complete integrity proof. inventory_clients hashes selected executable bytes and runs bounded local version/help probes; probe errors become evidence, while hashing failures can abort final setup.

Custom environments and operational diagnosis

--use-runtime PATH accepts an environment directory or interpreter. For an interpreter it queries sys.prefix, then checks the Python major/minor ABI against the bundled lock. It runs core imports and, when required, the packaged inference check. It does not replace dependencies or publish a managed generation for that runtime. Acceptance/private-root preparation can still occur, and the launch owner can register the selected environment. Compatibility responsibility remains with the custom-runtime operator.

Use the compiled executable's --dependency-status --json to inspect published and pending results. --repair-dependencies retries dependency preparation; --setup returns after setup/registration rather than starting the application. Read the failed-step/check lists and retained command-log paths before deciding which prerequisite needs repair. Neither ready status nor a successful local client version probe establishes connectivity, credentials or permission for later tools.

Selected cases in compiled bootstrap tests exercise warm reuse without subprocesses/cache repair, elevated-run refusal, failed repair retaining the prior environment, pending resume, native-profile identity, interrupted venv/build setup, argument preservation, client extraction, manager selection and environment filtering. These fixtures mock installers and network operations; they do not certify a live OS installation or all feature checks. No installation, package-manager operation or model workload was launched for this documentation review.
